common_name: Electric Plum Heuchera (Silver-Overlaid Purple-Black Coral Bells)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Electric Plum is a Terra Nova Nurseries selection bred for intensely dark, ruffled foliage with a distinctive metallic sheen.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; too much hot afternoon sun can scorch the thin, ruffled leaves, while deep shade mutes the color contrast. Electric Plum produces deeply lobed, heavily ruffled leaves in a near-black purple base overlaid with a silvery-pewter sheen that catches light differently than the flatter purple tones of older dark heucheras. Airy sprays of small cream-white flowers rise on wiry stems above the foliage in late spring and draw hummingbirds and small pollinators. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, discarding the older woody center and replanting the vigorous outer offsets.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heuchera for Southern Gardens

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Spellbound is a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction grown for its heavily ruffled, frosty rose-silver foliage.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with consistent moisture. Spellbound carries rounded, heavily ruffled leaves in a frosty silver-rose overlay with darker purple veining showing through underneath, giving the foliage a shimmering, almost metallic texture that shifts with the light and season. Small pale pink flowers appear on thin stems in late spring above the foliage. As with most silver-leaf heucheras, morning sun with afternoon shade brings out the brightest color without scorching the delicate leaf surface. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep the clump vigorous and well-shaped.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; like other Heuchera villosa selections, Freckles tolerates summer heat and humidity better than many hybrid coral bells.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; good air circulation and drainage help this fuzzy-leaved selection resist the crown rot that can trouble heucheras in heavy, wet soils. Freckles bears the soft, hairy, lobed leaves typical of the Southeastern native Heuchera villosa, speckled across the green surface with small cream to pale yellow dots that give the foliage a dappled, freckled appearance unlike the solid-colored leaves of most garden heucheras. Tall, airy sprays of small white flowers rise well above the foliage in mid to late summer, later than most heuchera cultivars. Its villosa parentage makes it notably more tolerant of heat, humidity, and heavier soils than many of the hybrid dark-leaf cultivars.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heuchera for Southern Gardens

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Chatterbox is an older coral bells selection grown primarily for its long season of rose-pink bloom rather than foliage color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, with afternoon shade appreciated in hotter climates. Chatterbox forms a neat mound of rounded, mottled green leaves topped from late spring through much of summer by slender, wiry stems carrying abundant small bell-shaped flowers in a clear rose-pink — one of the more free-flowering older Heuchera sanguinea selections, with a longer bloom season than many modern foliage-focused hybrids. Deadheading spent flower stems encourages continued bloom and keeps the planting tidy. Hummingbirds are frequent visitors to the nectar-rich flowers. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to renew vigor and flowering.

common_name: Coral Cloud Coral Bells (Coral-Red Flowering Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Coral Cloud is an older Heuchera sanguinea selection valued for its airy, abundant coral-red flower display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Coral Cloud sends up tall, slender flower stems in late spring and early summer carrying dense, airy clusters of small coral-red bells well above a low mound of rounded, lightly mottled green leaves, living up to its name with a hazy cloud-like mass of bloom color visible from a distance. The flowers are long-lasting both in the garden and as a cut flower, and regular deadheading extends the display into midsummer. It is a reliable, easy-care perennial for the front of a border or along a partly shaded path where hummingbirds can be enjoyed at close range. Divide every three to four years in spring to maintain a vigorous, floriferous clump.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; June Bride is a white-flowered Heuchera sanguinea selection that brightens the early-summer border.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. June Bride produces abundant sprays of small, pure white bell-shaped flowers on slender stems held above a tidy mound of rounded, lightly veined green leaves, offering a crisper contrast than the pink- or red-flowered sanguinea selections it is often paired with in mixed plantings. Bloom is heaviest in late spring into early summer, and deadheading the spent stems can coax out a lighter secondary flush. The clean white flowers pair well with blue- and purple-flowered companions and show up clearly in shaded garden areas at dusk. Divide every three to four years in spring to keep plants vigorous and well-flowered.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; Wu-La-La shares breeding with the giant 'Empress Wu' but matures to a more manageable scale.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade. Wu-La-La forms a large, dense mound of heavily corrugated leaves with bright gold-green centers framed by wide, dark green margins, a bolder and faster-maturing alternative to its all-green giant relatives for gardeners who want outsized scale without as many years of waiting. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in summer above the foliage. Consistent moisture and rich, well-amended soil support the large leaf size, and deep shade keeps the gold centers from bleaching in hot climates. Established clumps resent frequent disturbance and are best left to bulk up for several years between divisions.

common_name: Rhino Hide Hosta (Extremely Thick-Substance Blue-Green Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Rhino Hide was selected for exceptionally thick, tough leaf substance that resists slug feeding better than most hostas.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Rhino Hide forms a vigorous mound of thick, puckered, blue-green leaves whose unusually heavy substance makes the foliage noticeably more resistant to slug and snail damage than thinner-leaved hostas, a genuinely useful trait in damp, shaded gardens. The leaves hold their blue-green color well into summer before gradually greening as the waxy bloom wears away. Pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage on tall scapes in midsummer. It is a reliable, fast-bulking choice for gardeners who want the look of a classic blue hosta with fewer pest problems.

common_name: Orange Crush Hosta (Gold-Leaved Hosta with Orange-Red Petioles)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Orange Crush is grown for the contrast between its bright gold leaves and vivid orange-red petioles.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning sun to bring out the brightest gold leaf color. Orange Crush produces rounded, corrugated leaves that mature to a bright gold-chartreuse, set off by petioles and leaf bases in a striking orange-red that is unusual among hostas, most of which have plain green stems. The color contrast is most vivid in cooler spring and fall weather and in a site with some direct morning light. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes in summer. It combines well with blue-leaved and dark-foliage companions that set off both the gold leaves and the colorful stems.

common_name: Holy Mouse Ears Hosta (Streaked Sport of Blue Mouse Ears)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Holy Mouse Ears is a streaked sport of 'Blue Mouse Ears' prized among hosta collectors for its irregular creamy variegation.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Holy Mouse Ears arose as a sport of the popular miniature 'Blue Mouse Ears' and carries the same thick, rounded, slug-resistant blue-green leaves overlaid with irregular creamy-white streaking that varies from leaf to leaf and even within a single leaf. Because the variegation pattern is unstable, individual divisions can look noticeably different from one another, which is part of its appeal to collectors. Lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer. Its tiny mature size makes it well suited to troughs, rock gardens, and other small-scale shaded plantings.

common_name: Lemon Mouse Ears Hosta (Miniature Gold-Leaved Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Lemon Mouse Ears is a gold-leaved relative of 'Blue Mouse Ears' that keeps its bright color with some morning sun.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with filtered morning light to support the best gold color. Lemon Mouse Ears shares the thick, rounded, heavy-substance leaves of the Mouse Ears line but in a bright lemon-yellow to chartreuse tone that holds up well through the season rather than fading to green. Its diminutive, tight-mounding habit makes it a favorite for containers, troughs, and the front edge of a mixed shade planting, where its color provides a bright accent against darker-leaved neighbors. Pale lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer. It divides slowly, so mature clumps take time to bulk up.

common_name: Eternal Flame Hosta (Gold-Centered Hosta with Red-Tinted Petioles)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Eternal Flame is part of a modern hosta breeding trend toward colorful petioles and stem bases in addition to leaf variegation.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some morning light to deepen the leaf and petiole color. Eternal Flame produces broad, gently corrugated leaves with glowing gold to chartreuse centers framed by blue-green margins, while the petioles and lower leaf bases take on a warm reddish tint that intensifies through the season — a combination that gives the whole plant a subtle flame-like gradient of color. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in summer. As with other gold-centered hostas, some morning sun brings out the brightest color while deep, dense shade keeps the center more uniformly chartreuse-green.

common_name: Wheels of Light Hosta (Twisted-Margin Gold-Centered Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Wheels of Light is grown for its distinctively twisted, wavy leaf margins.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Wheels of Light produces rounded leaves with gold to chartreuse centers and narrow green margins that twist and ripple outward in a spiraling, spoke-like pattern unlike the flatter leaves of most hosta cultivars, giving established clumps a distinctive, almost sculptural texture even from a distance. Pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage on tall scapes in midsummer. The twisted margins are most pronounced on mature, well-established plants, so clumps become more dramatic and distinctive with each passing year. It pairs well with bold, solid-textured companions that set off its unusual leaf form.

common_name: Puddle Jumper Hosta (Small Thick-Substance Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Puddle Jumper is a small, heavy-substance blue hosta well suited to the front of a shaded border.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Puddle Jumper forms a dense, rounded mound of thick, cupped, powdery blue-green leaves with heavy substance that resists slug damage better than many thinner-leaved small hostas. Its compact habit and smaller mature size make it easy to tuck into the front of a shaded border, along a shaded walkway, or into a large container, where its texture and color read clearly without needing the space a full-size hosta demands. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes just above the foliage in summer. It bulks up at a moderate pace, dividing cleanly every few years in spring.

common_name: Mini Mouse Hosta (Tiny Blue-Green Miniature Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Mini Mouse is one of the smallest hostas in the Mouse Ears breeding line, staying true-miniature for years.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Mini Mouse forms an exceptionally tight, dense mound of small, thick, blue-green leaves, among the smallest mature sizes found in the Mouse Ears hosta lineage, making it well suited to troughs, miniature gardens, and the smallest scale rock-garden plantings where even 'Blue Mouse Ears' would look oversized. Despite its diminutive stature the leaves retain the heavy substance typical of the group, giving reasonable resistance to slug feeding. Lavender flowers appear on very short scapes in summer, close to the foliage. Clumps bulk up slowly and divide easily once large enough to split.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Queen Josephine combines a bright gold center with a wide blue-green margin on substantial, thick leaves.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with filtered morning light to bring out the fullest gold color in the leaf center. Queen Josephine forms a substantial mound of thick, corrugated leaves with glowing gold-chartreuse centers bordered by a wide, contrasting blue-green margin, a bold two-tone combination that reads well even at a distance in a shaded border. Pale lavender flowers rise on tall scapes above the foliage in summer. The thick leaf substance gives reasonably good resistance to slug damage for a gold-centered cultivar, and the plant bulks up at a steady, moderate pace once established.
